title: 6.2 Building and Optimizing an MMM
text:
Key Takeaways

MMM estimates channel contribution using aggregate data. It does not need user-level tracking, so it is resilient to cookie deprecation, App Tracking Transparency, and walled-garden limits.
Hill saturation and geometric adstock are the two main transforms. Each channel gets its own set of parameters.
Optimize based on marginal ROAS, not average ROAS. A channel with high average ROAS might already be deep into its saturation curve. Shifting dollars to a channel that is still on the steep part of its curve can increase total return, even if its average ROAS is lower.
Data requirements are specific: weekly data, at least 2–3 years of history, and real spend variation for each channel.
Bayesian estimation is now the default. Priors let you encode domain knowledge, and the posterior gives credible intervals instead of just point estimates.

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Geo-Lift Tests
The MMM in Section 6.2 measures, simulates, and optimizes, but its estimates are fundamentally observational. The model observes that weeks with higher TikTok spend tend to have higher sales, and attributes part of that lift to TikTok. It cannot, by itself, distinguish genuine media effects from confounders: seasonal demand that coincides with campaign flights, promotions that run alongside media pushes, or competitive dynamics that move several variables at once.
MMM also has a structural identification problem. Media channels are usually correlated: brands raise spend across all of them during the same peak periods. When Meta, Google, and TikTok spend all spike in Q4, the model cannot cleanly separate their individual effects. The result is wide credible intervals and unstable ROAS estimates.
Controlled experiments close the gap. A geo-lift test measures the causal incremental effect of a specific channel by varying spend across test and control geos. Feeding that estimate back into the MMM as an informative prior tightens the posterior and anchors one channel’s ROAS in experimental evidence.
This section walks through the loop: design the experiment, estimate the lift, convert it to a prior, plug it back into the model, and run calibration as a continuous program.
Companion notebook: sec6.2_mmm_end_to_end_demo.ipynb is shared with Section 6.2. Its Steps 14–17 implement this chapter’s calibration loop: convert a geo-lift estimate into a prior, refit the model, and re-optimize the budget.
View on GitHub
The most practical experiment design for MMM calibration is the geo-lift test (also called a matched-market test). Divide your markets into test and control groups, increase (or decrease) spend in the target channel for the test group, and measure the difference in outcomes.
Why geo-level? Because MMM operates at the geo-week level. A geo-lift test produces an estimate at the same granularity as the model’s inputs, making integration natural.
A typical design involves five decisions:
crumbs: 18  6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Target channel. Prioritize channels with the widest credible intervals in the uncalibrated model, or channels where the optimizer recommends large shifts.
Test and control geos. Split markets into groups with similar pre-period revenue trends. Parallel trends is the foundation of the DiD estimator: if test geos were already growing faster before the experiment, the estimate will be biased.
Intervention magnitude. A 5% spend increase is unlikely to produce a detectable signal in noisy weekly geo data. 20–50% is more typical.
Duration. Four to eight weeks of treatment is common. Include a pre-period of similar length for the parallel trends check.
Geo assignment. Pair up markets that look alike (similar size and similar pre-period trend), then randomize within each pair. Power comes from how much of the KPI the test group covers and how long the test runs, not from putting the biggest markets on one side. A size-lopsided split is exactly what breaks the parallel-trends check in step 2. If markets differ widely in size, analyze per-capita or log outcomes.

experiment:
  target_channel: TikTok
  spend_multiplier: 1.2        # +20% spend in test geos
  pre_weeks: 4
  geo_assignment:
    test: [DE, IT, NL, SE]        # mix large and small markets on each side
    control: [FR, ES, BE, AT, DK]
  periods:
    experiment_start: "2025-07-07"
    experiment_end: "2025-09-29"

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
From Lift to ROAS
The standard estimator for geo-lift tests is Difference-in-Differences (DiD): compare the change in revenue from pre to post in test geos against the same change in control geos. The DiD coefficient \(\hat{\beta}\) is average incremental revenue per geo-week. Convert to ROAS:
\[\text{ROAS}_{\text{lift}} = \frac{\hat{\beta} \times n_{\text{geos}} \times n_{\text{weeks}}}{\sum \Delta \text{spend}_{g,t}}\]






WarningMarginal ROAS, not average ROAS



This is a marginal ROAS (the return on the incremental dollar), not the average return across all dollars spent. The distinction is critical when converting the estimate to a prior, because the MMM posterior reflects average ROAS. We unpack this in the next section before showing the integration code.


Before using the estimate for calibration, verify three things: (1) parallel trends hold in the pre-period; (2) the ROAS estimate is positive; (3) the 95% CI is narrow enough to be useful as an anchor.
crumbs: 18  6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Marginal vs. Average ROAS
This point deserves emphasis because it is the most common source of confusion in calibration.
The geo-lift experiment measures marginal ROAS: the return on the incremental dollar of spend above the baseline level. The MMM posterior for roi_m reflects average ROAS: total media-driven revenue divided by total spend over the modeling period. Because of the Hill saturation curve, these are different quantities.






Figure 2: Marginal vs. average ROAS on a saturation curve.



Under a saturation curve that passes through the origin and bends downward, average ROAS is never below marginal ROAS: the average still carries the productive early dollars, while the marginal dollar lands on the flattening part of the curve. On the steep part (an under-invested channel) the two are nearly equal. As the channel saturates, the gap widens: marginal ROAS falls toward zero while average ROAS declines much more slowly. In Figure 2, the origin slope (average ≈ 0.40) sits well above the tangent slope (marginal ≈ 0.16). With an S-shaped curve the ordering can flip at very low spend, but at realistic spend levels the concave regime is what matters.
This is why we cannot plug the experimental ROAS directly into the model as a tight prior. Doing so would force the average-ROAS parameter to take a value that only makes sense for the marginal dollar. The fix is to inflate the standard error of the experimental estimate before converting it to a prior, to give the posterior room to land somewhere between the marginal and average values, weighted by the data.

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Integration with Meridian
Meridian supports two calibration mechanisms:

Informative ROAS prior (roi_m): a channel-specific LogNormal prior based on experimental results. The prior multiplies into the posterior alongside the likelihood; think of it as adding pseudo-observations about that channel’s ROAS, with weight set by roi_sigma. If the observational data disagree strongly, the posterior can still move away, and the smaller the sigma, the more the experiment outweighs the MMM’s own signal.
Calibration period (roi_calibration_period): a boolean array marking the experiment weeks. It does not add a separate constraint; it changes what the roi_m prior refers to, namely ROAS over the marked window rather than the whole modeling period, so the experimental estimate is compared against the quantity it actually measured.

Both mechanisms work together: the prior carries the experimental information, and the calibration period points it at the right window.
Converting the DiD estimate to a LogNormal prior. Note the se_inflated step: this is the marginal-vs-average adjustment we just discussed.
import numpy as np

def to_lognormal_params(mean, std):
    """Convert mean/std to LogNormal mu/sigma."""
    variance = std ** 2
    sigma_sq = np.log(1 + variance / mean ** 2)
    sigma = np.sqrt(sigma_sq)
    mu = np.log(mean) - sigma_sq / 2
    return mu, sigma

# Example: DiD estimate → LogNormal prior
roas_hat = 5.78  # DiD estimate
roas_se  = 3.73  # DiD standard error

# Inflate SE for the marginal-vs-average gap, then convert. Floor the
# LogNormal sigma (not the SE) so the floor is scale-free: no experiment,
# however tight, should claim less than ~30% multiplicative uncertainty
# about year-round ROAS. An absolute SE floor would behave very differently
# for a ROAS of 0.2 than for a ROAS of 6.
se_inflated = roas_se * 1.5
mu, sigma = to_lognormal_params(roas_hat, se_inflated)
sigma = max(sigma, 0.30)
# → mu ≈ 1.42, sigma ≈ 0.81
Setting channel-specific priors in Meridian:
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_probability as tfp
from meridian.model import prior_distribution, spec
from meridian import constants

channels = ["Meta", "Google", "TikTok", "TV", "OOH"]

# TikTok: calibrated from geo-lift experiment
# Others: default weakly informative prior
roi_mu    = tf.constant([0.20, 0.20, 1.42, 0.20, 0.20])
roi_sigma = tf.constant([1.00, 1.00, 0.81, 1.00, 1.00])

prior = prior_distribution.PriorDistribution(
    roi_m=tfp.distributions.LogNormal(
        loc=roi_mu,
        scale=roi_sigma,
        name=constants.ROI_M
    ),
)

model_spec = spec.ModelSpec(
    prior=prior,
    media_prior_type="roi",
    max_lag=12,
)
The calibrated channel should show a tighter credible interval and a posterior mean closer to the experimental estimate. Other channels may also benefit from reduced uncertainty, since tightening one channel helps the model attribute remaining variation more precisely.

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Running a Calibration Program
Calibration is not a one-time event. ROAS changes as audiences evolve, creative fatigues, and competitive dynamics shift.






Note



A practical annual cycle: Run the MMM in Q1, identify the channels with the widest credible intervals, run geo-lift tests in Q2–Q3, refresh the model in Q4 with calibrated priors. The Q4 model feeds into the next year’s budget planning.


Cost framing. A 20% spend increase in four geos for eight weeks may cost $50K–$200K. Frame this as an investment in decision quality. On a $100M media budget, correcting one channel’s ROAS by a single point on even 2% of spend ($2M) is worth about $2M a year, an order of magnitude above the experiment cost. The payoff comes from acting on a number you can trust, not from the experiment itself.
When calibration fails. Sometimes the DiD estimate is negative, nonsensical, or excessively noisy. Common causes: parallel trends violation, insufficient spend change, or external shocks during the test period. When this happens, do not force the estimate into the model. An unreliable calibration is worse than no calibration. Diagnose, adjust, and try again.
Calibration is iterative: better data → better models → better experiments → better data, looping each annual planning cycle.

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Reliability Checklist
Calibration makes MMM more useful, but it does not automatically make every recommendation trustworthy. Before sharing budget recommendations with a CMO or CFO, run the model through a short reliability checklist. The goal is not to prove that the model is perfect. The goal is to catch the issues that would make the optimizer’s output unsafe to use.

Data Quality

Enough history. Use at least two years of weekly data when possible. With fewer than 80 weekly observations, it becomes difficult to estimate adstock and saturation reliably.
Real variation in spend. Only include channels where spend actually moves. If a channel spends the same amount every week, the model has little signal to estimate its effect.
Correlated media flights. Check whether channels move together. If Meta, Google, TV, and TikTok all spike in the same weeks, the model may struggle to separate their individual effects.



Model Design

Controls for non-media demand. Include seasonality, holidays, promotions, pricing, distribution, and other business drivers where relevant. Otherwise, the model may attribute normal demand spikes to media.
Reasonable response curves. Inspect saturation and adstock curves. If a curve implies extreme lift from tiny spend changes, or no diminishing returns at all, the model may be fitting noise.
No unsafe extrapolation. Treat optimizer recommendations cautiously when they push spend far outside the historical range. MMM is much more reliable for interpolation than extrapolation.



Validation

Predictive performance. Check both in-sample and out-of-sample fit. A strong in-sample fit alone is not enough.
Uncertainty. Look at credible intervals, not just point estimates. Wide intervals are a warning that the channel’s ROAS is not well identified.
Experiment consistency. Compare MMM estimates against geo-lift or holdout results where available. If the two disagree materially, investigate before using the model for budget reallocation. Section 6.4 provides a protocol for working through these disagreements.

If the model passes these checks, the optimizer’s output is a reasonable starting point for planning. If it fails several of them, the right next step is not to optimize harder. It is to improve the data, redesign the model, or run a better calibration experiment.

title: 6.3 Calibrating MMM with Experiments
text:
Key Takeaways

MMM estimates are observational; experiments provide causal anchors. A geo-lift test can anchor one channel’s estimate and make downstream budget recommendations more trustworthy.
Geo-lift matches the model’s granularity. MMM operates at the geo-week level, and geo-lift produces estimates at the same level.
Marginal ROAS is not the same as average ROAS. The experiment measures the incremental dollar, while the MMM estimates average return. Inflate the standard error to give the posterior room to reconcile the two.
Calibration is iterative. One to two experiments per year, rotating across channels, is more realistic than trying to validate every channel at once.
Do not use the optimizer blindly. Before sharing recommendations, check data quality, model design, uncertainty, extrapolation risk, and consistency with experiments.

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
Why the Numbers Differ by Construction
Return to the CFO question from Section 6.1, one year and a full measurement stack later. Attribution reports a ROAS of 4.2 for retargeting and almost nothing for TV. The MMM credits TV/CTV with a meaningful share of conversion volume and estimates retargeting’s average ROAS at 1.8. A geo-lift test on retargeting comes back at an incremental ROAS of 0.9.
It is common to wonder which tool is wrong when the numbers do not match. In practice, attribution, MMM, and experiments are designed to answer different questions, using different data and time frames. Disagreement is normal and signals that each tool is doing its job.
The bigger risk is not disagreement, but inaction. The following sections explain why these conflicts happen, outline the three most common types of disagreement, and provide practical steps for making decisions even when the tools do not agree.
Most conflicts trace back to four structural differences between the tools.
Instead of asking which number is right, ask which number is built for the decision in front of you. The rest of this chapter focuses on the three types of conflicts you are most likely to encounter in practice.
crumbs: 19  6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
Source of disagreement
What it means in practice




Time windows
Attribution evaluates short click and view windows. MMM, through adstock, captures carryover that plays out over weeks; Section 6.2 modeled TV with a 6-week half-life. A four-week test measures only what happens inside the test.


Data inputs
Attribution sees user-level tracked paths, and misses whatever tracking misses. MMM sees aggregate spend and revenue. Experiments see the difference between test and control geos.


Estimand
Attribution distributes observed conversions across touchpoints. MMM estimates each channel’s average contribution by regression. Experiments estimate the incremental effect of one specific spend change. These are three different definitions of “effectiveness.”


External factors
MMM explicitly controls for seasonality, promotions, and macro drivers. Attribution does not. Experiments difference them out through the control group.
crumbs: 19  6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
section: Attribution Says Cut, MMM Says Keep
text:
Attribution Says Cut, MMM Says Keep
This is the most common conflict. Attribution concentrates credit on lower-funnel channels that sit close to the conversion event: paid search, retargeting, affiliates. Upper-funnel channels create demand that surfaces later as branded search or direct traffic, so their contribution is invisible in path data while remaining visible to the MMM as aggregate lift.
The standard scenario: attribution suggests cutting upper-funnel spend that “never shows up in converting paths,” while the MMM attributes a meaningful share of conversion volume to those same channels.
How to act: Match the tool to the decision. Use the calibrated MMM for cross-channel budget allocation and to set channel-level guardrails. Use attribution for within-channel decisions like creative testing, keyword bidding, or audience selection. In meetings, clarify whether you are making a budget decision or an execution decision.
crumbs: 19  6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
The Test Contradicts Attribution
Experiments are the ground truth for incrementality, and they can break against attribution in either direction.
The test shows less than attribution claims. Attribution counts users who would have converted anyway. Retargeting is the canonical case: it targets people who already visited the site, so the tracked paths are full of conversions that the ads did not cause.
The test shows more than attribution claims. Channels with weak tracking coverage (CTV, streaming audio, much of YouTube) are underrepresented or absent in path data. Attribution reports near-zero contribution because it literally cannot see the exposures, while a geo holdout reveals meaningful incremental lift.
How to act: Use experiments to make go/no-go decisions about whether a channel deserves investment. Continue to use attribution for tactical decisions in channels where tracking is reliable. If there is a large gap between tested and attributed ROAS, treat it as a signal about where your tracking is incomplete, not as a sign that one tool is broken.
crumbs: 19  6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
The Test Contradicts the MMM
This is the subtler conflict, because both tools claim to measure incremental contribution. The typical shape: the MMM, fit on two to three years of weekly data, shows a channel as effective; a four-to-eight-week geo test on the same channel shows little or no lift.
Two mechanisms explain most of these gaps. The first is time horizons. Through adstock, the MMM picks up carryover and slow-building brand effects that a short test window structurally cannot observe. The test is not wrong; it is answering a shorter-run question. The second is operating points. The MMM’s coefficients describe average behavior over the historical spend range, while the test perturbs spend at one specific point on the saturation curve.
How to act: Use the experimental result to calibrate the MMM, as described in Section 6.3. Focus on whether the estimates are directionally consistent, rather than expecting them to match exactly.

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
A Decision Protocol
The three conflicts resolve the same way: identify which tool owns the decision at stake, act on that tool’s number, and treat the disagreement itself as information about where to test next. The table below summarizes the playbook.









Situation
Trust most
Decision at stake
Action




Attribution says cut, the MMM says keep
The calibrated MMM, plus a follow-up test
Upper-funnel budget
Do not cut outright; schedule a geo test on the disputed channel


Attribution says strong, the test says weak
The experiment
Channel incrementality
Cap or scale back spend; retargeting is the classic case


The MMM says strong, the test says weak
Both, allowing for the horizon gap
Calibration
Widen the experimental prior; check the test window against the channel’s adstock


All three are uncertain
No single tool
Risk management
Hold the budget steady and design the experiment that narrows the widest interval



A protocol only works if it is agreed on before the numbers arrive. Fix the decision rules in advance: who owns which decision, and what evidence is good enough to act on. Then run the meetings against deadlines, not against convergence: bring ranges rather than point estimates, make the call on schedule, and feed the gap between prediction and outcome into the next round of experiments.

title: 6.4 When Attribution, MMM, and Experiments Disagree
text:
Key Takeaways

Attribution, MMM, and experiments measure different quantities, over different windows, from different data. Disagreement is structural, and a stack whose tools always agreed would be redundant.
Route conflicts by decision type: the calibrated MMM owns cross-channel budget guardrails, experiments own channel go/no-go, and attribution owns in-channel tactics.
When a test undercuts attribution, suspect selection on intent (retargeting is the canonical case). When a test exceeds attribution, suspect tracking gaps (CTV, streaming). Both gaps are information about your data, not errors in your tools.
When a test contradicts the MMM, check the time horizons and the operating point on the saturation curve, then calibrate rather than replace (Section 6.3).
Fix the decision rules before the numbers arrive: who owns which decision, and what is good enough to act on. Bring ranges to the meeting, decide on schedule rather than waiting for the numbers to converge, and feed the gap between prediction and outcome into the next experiment.

title: Closing Thoughts
text:
We opened this book with a claim: analysis creates value only when it changes a decision, an action, and ultimately a business result. Every chapter since has been a different way of keeping that promise.

Looking back, each part handed you a different lever:

Part 1 showed what makes marketing data its own discipline: the funnel, the datasets, and the three characteristics that shape every analysis.
Part 2 turned analysis around to start from the decision: the business question, the KPI tree, and a story that ends in an action.
Part 3 separated causation from correlation: experiments where you can randomize, quasi-experiments where you cannot, and uplift models to target the customers who actually change their behavior.
Part 4 asked who your customers are and what each relationship is worth.
Part 5 priced the products, chose the assortment, and forecast the demand.
Part 6 followed the money: attribution, MMM, the experiments that keep an MMM honest, and what to do when those tools disagree.

The methods differ, but the discipline is the same: name the decision first, then choose the method.
A second thread runs through the book: none of these models is ever finished. The useful ones are calibrated against experiments, checked for reliability, and kept close to the decision they serve. That is why Part 6 included a reliability checklist rather than a victory lap, and it is the habit I most hope you take away.
Where to go from here:

Run the notebooks against your own data. The Notebooks & Code appendix lists all of them; every one runs on public datasets you can swap out.
Go deeper on any chapter. Further Reading collects the books, papers, and repositories behind each part.
Say hello. Open an issue on GitHub, or find me on LinkedIn.

Tools will keep changing. The questions will not: did it work, and what should we do next? If this book helps you answer them a little more honestly, it has done its job.
Thank you for reading.

title: Further Reading
text:
What is Marketing Science?

Provost, F. & Fawcett, T. (2013). Data Science for Business. O’Reilly Media. Frames data science around business decisions rather than model accuracy, the book’s core stance; worth revisiting here in Part 1.

Three Characteristics of Marketing Data

Part 3: Causal Inference for Marketing

Causal Thinking & Selection Bias

This is the book’s curated bibliography: the academic papers, books, and library documentation that underpin the methods presented throughout. Entries are generated from references.bib and ordered alphabetically by author. For recommended and supplementary readings organized by topic, see Further Reading.


Brodersen, Kay H, Fabian Gallusser, Jim Koehler, Nicolas Remy, and
Steven L Scott. 2015. “Inferring Causal Impact Using
Bayesian Structural Time-Series Models.” The
Annals of Applied Statistics 9 (1): 247–74.


Bult, Jan Roelf, and Tom Wansbeek. 1995. “Optimal Selection for
Direct Mail.” Marketing Science 14 (4): 378–94.


Chan, David, and Matthew Perry. 2017. Challenges and Opportunities
in Media Mix Modeling. Google Inc. https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/45998.pdf.


Deng, Alex, Ya Xu, Ron Kohavi, and Toby Walker. 2013. “Improving
the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing
Pre-Experiment Data.” Proceedings of the Sixth ACM
International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM ’13),
123–32. https://doi.org/10.1145/2433396.2433413.


Fader, Peter S, and Bruce GS Hardie. 2013. The Gamma-Gamma Model of
Monetary Value. Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania. https://www.brucehardie.com/notes/025/gamma_gamma.pdf.


Fader, Peter S, Bruce GS Hardie, and Ka Lok Lee. 2005. “Counting
Your Customers the Easy Way: An Alternative to the Pareto/NBD
Model.” Marketing Science 24 (2): 275–84.


Jin, Yuxue, Yueqing Wang, Yunting Sun, David Chan, and Jim Koehler.
2017. Bayesian Methods for Media Mix Modeling with Carryover and

Visualization Guide for Business Professionals. Wiley.

P&G Is Taking to Improve the Media Supply
Chain.” https://www.pg.co.uk/blogs/PritchardANA2019/.

Business. O’Reilly Media.

Vaver, Jon, and Jim Koehler. 2011. Measuring Ad Effectiveness Using
Geo Experiments. Google Inc. https://research.google/pubs/pub38355/.


Vizard, Sarah. 2019. “P&G Shifts from Targeting
‘Generic Demographics’ to ‘Smart
Audiences’.” Marketing Week, July. https://www.marketingweek.com/pg-targeting-generic-demographics-to-smart-audiences/.


Xie, Huizhi, and Juliette Aurisset. 2016. “Improving the
